#5315. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5314. NAR President Kevin Brown warns of outside forces threatening real estate marketplace

Outgoing NAR President Kevin Brown defended the MLS model as central to transparency and competition while warning that outside interests could seek more control of the marketplace. He also addressed NAR reforms, legislative priorities and member accountability ahead of a leadership transition.  AI Summary

As his term as president of the National Association of Realtors (NAR) comes to a close, Kevin Brown is warning real estate professionals that outside forces seeking greater control of the industry could threaten the transparency and competition that are the backbone of the current real estate marketplace.

In remarks prepared for NAR NXT in New Orleans this week, Brown drew parallels between the forces that contributed to the 2008 housing crisis and those he believes are now attempting to reshape how real estate is bought and sold.

“Today, outside forces have once again entered our industry, and this time around it is our marketplace instead of our financial system, motivated by profits, control and market share,” Brown said.

He did not identify the companies or organizations he was referring to, but his comments come as the industry debates the future of listing distribution, broker control of listing data and the role of multiple listing services (MLSs).

Brown said he believes the MLS system remains essential to maintaining competition and giving buyers and sellers access to comprehensive property information.

“America is home to the fairest, most accessible and transparent real estate market in the world,” Brown said. “That is because of a pro-competitive foundation that provides the broadest, most reliable view of the market, anchored in the MLS system.”

Perhaps in a nod to the increase in private listings, he emphasized that consumer choice depends not only on the ability to make decisions but also on access to the information needed to make them.

“A fair and transparent marketplace gives homebuyers and sellers both choice and clarity — the freedom to choose and the information to understand the consequences of that choice,” he said.

According to Brown, NAR is working with MLSs, associations and industry leaders to address marketplace concerns while advocating for the MLS system in Washington.

He also urged members to take a more active role in defending the existing marketplace. “Be prepared to support and defend a marketplace that doesn’t just benefit a select few, but a marketplace that serves us all — the consumer, the industry and Realtors,” Brown said.

When it comes to the association, Brown acknowledged shortcomings. “If NAR wants to lead change, we must be willing to change ourselves,” Brown said. “We cannot wait for outside forces to set our agenda or determine our direction.”

Brown pointed to organizational changes this year, including staff reductions, streamlined governance and a renewed focus on member services. These changes are part of NAR’s three-year strategic plan, which focuses on rebuilding the member experience and modernizing the association.

“That is why we have rightsized our staff, streamlined our governance structure and sharpened our focus,” he said. “But the real test is not whether we created a plan. It is whether that plan helps you get to your next transaction, better serve your clients and move our industry forward.”

Brown also strongly addressed criticism of NAR, acknowledging the association’s shortcomings while challenging critics to provide accurate information. “Accountability starts with being honest about where NAR has fallen short, what must change and whether we are delivering value for you,” Brown said.

But Brown also took aim at what he characterized as sensationalized coverage of the association. “For some, reporting on NAR’s progress is not a profitable story. Sensationalism sells,” Brown said. “We are not interested in fueling miscommunication and half-truths to boost views, profits or egos.”

Brown maintained that criticism is necessary but said it must be grounded in facts. “We respect our critics,” he said. “Honest criticism makes us better and helps hold us accountable.”

Brown also highlighted NAR’s legislative efforts, including passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

“It took Realtors to get it across the finish line,” Brown said. He also pointed to efforts to modernize credit scoring and help delinquent veteran homeowners avoid foreclosure.

As Brown prepares to hand over the presidency to Florida’s Christine Hansen, he acknowledged that the association still has work to do. “NAR is not perfect and our work is not finished,” he said.

And while he warns that criticism of the association should be based on facts, he insists that members continue to hold NAR accountable. “Keep asking us the hard questions,” Brown said. “Keep holding us responsible for clear communication and meaningful results.”

#5313. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5312. Atomicwork launches certified AI coworker marketplace for enterprise IT and security

Information technology service management startup Atomicwork Inc. today announced the launch of an Artificial Intelligence Coworker Marketplace that will give enterprise IT and security teams access to prebuilt, certified AI coworkers that can work alongside employees.

The company said these agentic AI coworkers include verified roles and capabilities across cloud infrastructure, access management, security and device operations.

“Most AI-native ITSM vendors today don’t have much to show for their agents’ effectiveness — a listing means ‘this agent works,’ not ‘this AI Agent has real, verified coverage of the systems it needs to touch and has been tested and fine-tuned using real-world enterprise use cases,’ which has made enterprises wary of agentic claims,” co-founder and Chief Executive Vijay Rayapati told SiliconANGLE.

Founded in 2022, Atomicwork began with the premise that information technology and security teams face challenging, process-intensive work and long tasks that could be automated. To tackle these problems, the company evaluated its agentic coworkers against real enterprise use cases, giving organizations a faster way to deploy AI workers without developing or validating them from scratch.

The initial lineup of coworkers includes an enterprise operations AI coworker, along with a CloudOps engineer, AccessOps manager, SecOps manager and DeviceOps manager. These AI coworkers can work across enterprise systems including AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, Okta, Active Directory, Splunk and Google SecOps.

The company said every AI Coworker comes out of the box with the skills and integrations needed for its role, reducing the work IT teams would otherwise spend wiring up systems and validating procedures.

Every agent can be quickly tailored to internal infrastructure, company culture, specialized expertise and business logic. Using that, they can quickly generate and tackle large volumes of recurring operational work under the supervision of IT and security teams. The company added that administrators will retain full control of agent management, allowing them to decide what systems an agent can access, what actions it can perform and how those actions are governed.

The objective is not merely to provide a catalog of available agents with a card to explain their capabilities. Atomicwork’s certification verifies that each AI Coworker has the needed integrations and skill coverage for the role to get the work done before deployment.

Atomicwork said customers using access automation have already seen speed-ups, with applications that don’t require approval having a median turnaround of about 18 seconds, while those requiring approval have a turnaround of about 2.5 hours. In contrast, the industry standard, which can be heavily influenced by business maturity and the risk behind the application’s use, could take between a full day and three business days depending on the amount of automation behind the scenes.

The company said this marketplace represents the beginning of a broader plan to create an ecosystem of enterprise AI Coworkers, built and certified by Atomicwork. Third parties will also be able to contribute skills and integrations through its Model Context Protocol store and skill registry to enhance coworker capabilities.

“This launch is the first step toward a third-party AI Coworker marketplace, where partners publish their own coworkers and certify them against our enterprise bench,” said Rayapati.

#5310. Elizabeth Warren expected to lead Senate banking committee in January

Elizabeth Warren is expected to chair the Senate banking committee in January after Democrats flipped Congress. The role would expand her investigative authority and could increase scrutiny of banks, lenders, private equity and crypto, alongside oversight of CFPB changes.   AI Summary

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to become chair of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs when Democrats take control of Congress in January, giving the Massachusetts Democrat expanded authority to investigate financial institutions and advance legislation affecting the sector.

The move is expected as a result of this week’s midterm elections, which saw both the Senate and House of Representatives flip from Republican to Democratic majorities.

Several outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and Reuters, anticipate that Warren is lined up for the role, even though other senators could theoretically rank ahead of her for the chairmanship.

The transition would give Warren, who is currently a ranking member of the legislative committee, more staff and subpoena powers, potentially increasing scrutiny of major banks, consumer lenders, private equity firms and cryptocurrency companies.

Warren, who would replace current Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.), is also expected to examine the Trump administration’s mass firings of financial regulatory employees and potential conflicts of interest involving companies with ties to the president.

Warren has built her political career around financial regulation and consumer protection. A former Harvard University law professor and bankruptcy expert, she became involved in developing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in the wake of the great financial crisis under President Barack Obama before winning a Senate seat in 2012.

Her expected chairmanship comes as the CFPB faces significant operational challenges and restructuring under the Trump administration, a move that she has publicly criticized.

The administration, meanwhile, has argued that the CFPB over-regulates consumer lenders and has been used to target political opponents and disfavored industries, going so far as to scale back enforcements this year.

The CFPB has undergone a leadership shuffle as a result of the administration’s efforts to scale back the agency’s power. In September, the committee advanced the nomination of Brian Johnson, Trump’s newest nominee to become director of the bureau, a move that Warren opposed.

#5309. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5308. Massachusetts AG issues rule on shared appreciation mortgages, NCLC calls for broader protections

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, a dual-lien structure that ties repayment to home price appreciation. The regulation clarifies when nonprofit lenders are shielded from consumer protection claims and requires stronger disclosures, including maximum potential repayment amounts. Stemming from a 2024 law that granted broad liability waivers to nonprofit SAMs such as BlueHub, the rule follows litigation alleging the products function as high-cost, subprime-style loans that can strip home equity.   AI Summary

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, adding disclosure and consumer protection requirements for a niche home equity product that has faced recent scrutiny.

The rule, effective Nov. 6, clarifies when nonprofit shared appreciation mortgage (SAM) lenders are shielded from state consumer protection claims and sets new notice standards, including prominent disclosure of the maximum amount borrowers may have to repay, according to an announcement from the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC).

The regulation stems from a provision in the state’s economic development bill, passed in November 2024. That statute carved out a broad waiver of liability under Massachusetts consumer protection laws for certain nonprofit SAMs, including loans originated by BlueHub Capital. Advocates say the legislative change created a “dangerous loophole” that exposed distressed homeowners to complex and costly loan structures with limited recourse.

Under the BlueHub-style model, borrowers typically receive a fixed-rate first mortgage alongside a second lien tied to future home price appreciation. The SAM second lien requires the homeowner to share a portion of any increase in property value with the lender upon sale, transfer or refinance. Because the payoff amount is variable and not set in dollars at origination, borrowers can face unexpectedly large balloon payments when they attempt to exit the loan.

NCLC noted that the risks of these structures have been highlighted in Humes v. BlueHub Capital Inc., a Massachusetts class-action lawsuit alleging SAMs embed hidden, subprime-level costs that can strip significant equity and accelerate home loss. The court found BlueHub liable for violating multiple state lending laws and recently certified the class to move forward, according to NCLC.

“While presented as a lifeline, shared appreciation mortgages often become a trap,” Andrea Bopp Stark, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said in a statement. “The AG’s final rule protects people from BlueHub’s loan model and similar products, but Massachusetts must go further to prevent harm from more common home equity theft loan products, including Home Equity Investment Loans.”

The AG’s new rule does not eliminate SAMs but seeks to ensure that nonprofit and other lenders using these instruments do so transparently and within defined consumer protection boundaries.

The regulation spells out the limited circumstances in which a SAM lender can be insulated from claims under Massachusetts consumer protection law and establishes a framework for robust disclosures, including clear presentation of the maximum possible repayment obligation.

While praising the change, NCLC argues that the rule does not reach a far enough to impact a growing category of products — home equity investments (HEIs). These provide upfront cash to a homeowner in exchange for a share of the future home price appreciation. NCLC characterized these arrangements as high risk for borrowers, as the actual amount owed depends on home price growth and triggers large, lump-sum obligations.

A representative at the AG’s office did not immediately respond to HousingWire‘s request for comment on the changes.

Massachusetts AG Andrea Joy Campbell has already challenged one HEI provider, Hometap. The state alleges consumer protection violations tied to HEI structures. But NCLC noted that the latest rulemaking in Massachusetts does not specifically regulate HEI products.

“The new rules provide important safeguards and requirements for SAMs, and stronger and broader rules are needed to address the high-risk HEI loans that are now targeting Massachusetts homeowners,” Bopp Stark said.

Consumers in other parts of the country have challenged HEI providers in court. Last year, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a 2023 judgment from a district court in Washington state, ruling that Unison‘s HEI product amounted to a reverse mortgage under state law.

In August, HEI provider Unlock settled with the Office of the Minnesota Attorney General over allegations that the company’s home equity agreements (HEAs) were mortgage loans that violated state usury caps, disclosure rules and licensing requirements.

Companies say they are supportive of regulatory efforts, pointing to a legal framework passed earlier this year in Illinois that could serve as model at the national level. At the Mortgage Bankers Association‘s Annual Convention & Expo last month, executives at Point told HousingWire they believe universal regulations are coming.

“We believe that these companies are going to be regulated,” said Dan McPheeters, Point’s head of business development and partnerships. “The practical effect is, it’s difficult to comply with [mortgage regulations] for a product that doesn’t have a monthly payment, that isn’t self-amortizing. … That said, as long as you address those tactical issues, this should be regulated.”

#5307. How a new Pulte Florida agrihood makes conservation a buyer desire

PulteGroup is developing The Grow, a 1,200-acre agrihood east of Orlando planned for about 2,200 homes anchored by a 9-acre working farm. Plans leave just over half the site undeveloped, positioning the project as a growth and conservation case study.  AI Summary

For years, Central Florida’s exploding population growth and rapidly expanding suburban sprawl have clashed with local efforts to protect the region’s dwindling green space and undeveloped land. PulteGroup’s new 1,200-acre community on Orlando’s eastern edge aims to balance these seemingly contradictory interests.

The community is called The Grow. Once undeveloped, rural land, the property is set to begin morphing into a roughly 2,200-home “agrihood” centered around a 9-acre working farm. In keeping with its conservation focus, the plan calls for reserving just over half of the site from development, including wetlands, conservation areas and shared green space.

The Grow offers a potential case study in balancing growth and conservation, a tension deeply felt in Central Florida and many other high-growth Sun Belt markets. Between 2000 and 2025, the Orlando metro area’s population grew nearly 80%, from 1.64 million to 2.95 million.

That growth reshaped once-rural communities on the region’s edges, replacing undeveloped land with new subdivisions, apartments and shopping centers. Many long-time Sunshine State residents now lament the loss of “Old Florida,” marked by a landscape of open land, working ranches and orange groves that are now developed.

When Pulte, the sole homebuilder at The Grow, purchased the community’s lots in 2023, it set out to build a premier community that responded to these tensions.

“One of our biggest selling features is the openness of the community and how much greenery we left. Everywhere you look, you’re surrounded by trees,” Patrick McNamara, a Sales Manager at Pulte, told HousingWire TBD.

However, the true distinguisher between The Grow and other local communities will be its working farm, a rare amenity that carries the conservation theme beyond protecting land to putting it to use.

For Pulte, which held a grand opening for the community in late September, the farm and the extensive conservation space give the builder a way to stand out to prospective homebuyers, a crucial edge considering the challenging sales environment homebuilders are facing.

The working farm is central to the community’s agrihood concept – providing fresh, sustainably grown produce. Residents will support it by buying products, volunteering and joining educational activities.

McNamara argued that the farm creates a direct connection between residents and their food. A professional third-party company will manage the farm, but residents and families will be allowed to volunteer and then buy the finished produce at a resident-only general store that will serve as an anchor for The Grow’s commercial and retail street.

The development will include two other farms: a small demonstration farm, covering about an eighth of an acre, and a separate community farm where homeowners can practice what they learn.

These smaller farms will serve as an educational, hands-on amenity for families, where residents can learn each stage of growing produce and then put what they learn into practice. An existing program, “Seed the Table,” will allow residents to plant crops, watch them grow and eat what they produced.

The farmers will also work with the lifestyle director to hold chef-led cooking classes at the community’s gathering barn, and will host seasonal celebrations and festivals that bring homeowners together.

Beyond conservation and sustainability, the farm is meant to build community, encourage learning and offer a unique lifestyle.

The Grow, which features homes from the low $400s to the high $800s, isn’t immune to the macro-level sales pressures impacting the local and national housing market. McNamara concedes that his team has to leverage generous incentives like mortgage rate buydowns to finish sales.

However, he also confirmed that The Grow has sold more than 100 homes since opening pre-sales about six months ago, and that prospective buyers have been anticipating the community’s opening for years.

The agrihood concept is the hook that draws buyers in.

“The farm is a big draw,” McNamara said. “I think the agrihood is what’s bringing people in, but what’s getting them to buy is once they see everything else that comes with it.”

In addition to the working farm and conservation space, The Grow will feature a main street with about 170,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, envisioned as a high-end retail and dining corridor that can work as a visitor magnet.

Other features include an indoor event and social space, an outdoor green space with a community pizza oven, a dedicated dog park, walking and nature trails, playgrounds and other resident-only amenities like a clubhouse, a gym and a pool.

“[Buyers] are shocked to find out that this isn’t a little farm community. This is a high-end resort neighborhood.”

The community’s preservation of nature is another big selling point. While many newly built communities lack mature trees and vegetation, The Grow’s preservation space means that residents can live alongside nature from day one.

“It’s really about getting immersed in nature, and that’s really hard to find in new construction,” McNamara said. “Homebuilders typically buy a piece of land and clear it out, start from scratch, and then plant a lot of trees. But you’ve got another 30 years until you can really enjoy the shade from it. In this neighborhood, we’ve left hundreds of 100-year-old oaks all throughout the community. We’ve made them focal points.”

“One of the big draws is the lifestyle and the outdoor feeling that you’re going to have in this community,” he added

#5306. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?

#5305. The AI boom’s missing balance-sheet question: What has actually been verified?

GUEST COLUMN by Neil P. Osnato

I spent 13 years on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. One lesson stayed with me long after the trading jackets disappeared: A transaction could be executed, documented and perfectly valid while the assumptions that made it attractive proved less durable than anyone expected.

That distinction matters in the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. We can believe AI will transform productivity and still ask whether each financing, data-center expansion or long-term capacity agreement is supported by evidence that can survive the investment’s life.

The industry is making commitments across different clocks. Compute contracts may run for years. Debt can mature decades from now.

Servers have much shorter technology cycles. Power infrastructure, transmission upgrades and buildings may outlast several generations of the equipment they were built to support. Meanwhile, enterprise customers are still learning what they will use, how intensively they will use it and what they will pay.

None of this proves the investments are unsound. It does create a question that belongs beside revenue forecasts and capital budgets: What exactly has been verified at the moment an institution decides to rely on a promise?

An agreement to purchase compute can be commercially meaningful. It may support financing and demonstrate customer commitment. But it does not by itself establish that the underlying workloads will remain economically productive at the contracted scale, or that the customer will renew on similar terms once technology and prices change.

A serious review must separate the existence of the contract from the economic assumptions behind its duration, usage profile, counterparty capacity and renewal expectations. Contract enforceability and economic durability are related; they are not interchangeable.

A data-center campus can be announced, financed and partially constructed before all of its necessary electricity, cooling, network and equipment dependencies have become operational. A power purchase agreement is not itself proof of deliverability at the exact commissioning date. GPU orders are not proof that a facility can run the ordered cluster at the planned duty cycle.

For infrastructure planning, I use a simple sequence: requested load, evidenced load, deliverable load, energized load, utilized load and sustained demand. These are not six fancy names for the same megawatt. They describe different claims, each requiring different supporting records.

That distinction is already relevant to public grid decisions. Persistence Analytics Group has submitted comments in MISO’s Large Load Working Group proceedings on load forecasts, application and study processes, paired-resource studies and cost transparency. The recurring question is how planners preserve alignment when a proposed project’s capacity, timing or other material conditions change after an earlier study or commitment.

Financial engineering can provide meaningful protection. Minimum payments, parent guarantees, collateral requirements, termination provisions and residual-value commitments can shift or mitigate losses. They should be evaluated on their actual terms and credit strength.

But a contractual remedy is not the same as the continued usefulness of the underlying asset. A guarantee may support recovery from a counterparty while leaving the investor dependent on that counterparty’s resources, enforceability, timing and the value remaining after a disruption. Those are separate assumptions that deserve separate evidence.

This is especially important when apparently distinct exposures rely on a small set of interconnected customers, infrastructure providers, funding sources or technology assumptions. Diversifying contracts does not necessarily diversify the dependency underneath them.

Initial diligence usually asks whether a project is supportable at approval. A more durable approach asks what must remain true afterward — and which changes require the original case to be revisited before additional money is committed.

Consider a campus whose customer delays its ramp, whose power availability moves to a later year or whose equipment changes materially. Each event may be manageable on its own. But if the original financing or infrastructure decision assumed the earlier configuration, someone must decide whether the updated evidence still supports the next commitment.

That is a decision gate, not a prediction about whether AI succeeds. It calls for a documented chain: the representation being relied upon; the assumption embedded in it; the evidence supporting that assumption; the dependencies that must hold; the party bearing downside exposure; and the material change that would require reassessment.

Different specialists own different pieces. Engineers assess technical deliverability. Lawyers assess contractual rights. Accountants and finance teams assess financial statements and cash flows. Independent decision assurance asks whether those records, taken together, actually establish the proposition the capital allocator is relying on — and whether known gaps have been made explicit.

The productive-utilization debate is essential. So is the question of who will pay for AI intelligence, and at what price. But before authorizing the next investment, a chief financial officer or investment committee can ask an even more immediate question: Which assumptions are verified facts, which are binding commitments, which are conditional forecasts and which need to be revalidated because something material has changed?

A sector can produce transformational technology and disappointing returns on some of its assets. We have seen that distinction in markets before. The lesson is not to stop investing. It is to stop treating execution, delivery, utilization and durable economic value as if they were the same event.

On the trading floor, the confirmation of a trade was the beginning of understanding the position, not the end. AI infrastructure deserves the same discipline.

Neil P. Osnato is founder of Persistence Analytics Group LLC, an independent Decision Assurance™ and Infrastructure Assumption Verification™ firm. He previously spent 13 years trading on the New York Stock Exchange floor. His work focuses on the documentary evidence supporting consequential infrastructure and financial decisions. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Selected public background: MISO Large Load Working Group stakeholder feedback (LLWG-2026-7 and LLWG-2026-8), September 2026; The Bond Buyer, “Deciding About Data Centers,” October 28, 2026.

#5304. Progress Residential to pay $49.8M to settle FTC, state claims over rental practices

Progress Residential, the single-family rental operator owned by Pretium Partners, agreed to a $49.8 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and state regulators over allegations it hid rental fees, mishandled security deposits and misled tenants about property conditions.   AI Summary

Progress Residential, the property manager of single-family rental homes owned by Pretium Partners, has agreed to pay $49.8 million to settle deceptive and unfair practices claims by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state regulators. The company denies any wrongdoing.

In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, regulators alleged that the company advertised rental prices that did not reflect the full amount tenants would be required to pay, imposed hidden or inadequately disclosed fees and charges, and mishandled security deposits.

The claims also included that Progress misrepresented the condition and move-in readiness of properties, restricted tenants’ ability to share reviews, and failed to adequately address tenant complaints and maintenance issues.

In a statement given to HousingWire, a representative of Progress Residential and Pretium said the companies have reached an agreement “with the FTC and four states to resolve the Commission’s Civil Investigative Demand related to certain aspects of our resident experience during the period of 2021 to 2025.”

“The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing, and we maintain Progress’ practices have been transparent, fair, and consistent with industry practice,” the spokesperson said. “Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our mission of expanding access to quality, affordable rental housing in neighborhoods of opportunity.”

The deal was reached by the FTC, the attorneys general of Arizona, Indiana and Colorado, and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection. It combines monetary relief for renters across the country.

“We will always welcome investment in housing and recognize the important role private capital can play in increasing opportunities for Hoosier families,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in a statement. “But no company, regardless of size or financial backing, gets a free pass to mislead consumers, impose hidden charges or treat tenants unfairly.”

“Consumers searching for housing should have access to straightforward information about the costs associated with renting a home,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Transparency regarding rental prices and fees helps consumers compare options and make informed choices. Clear pricing practices also support competition by allowing housing providers to compete on the basis of price, quality and service.

“The FTC is monitoring the rental housing market and will continue to take action where appropriate to ensure that consumers receive clear and accurate information about the costs of renting a home.”

Per the settlement terms, Progress must disclose the total monthly rental price in advertisements and listings, along with mandatory fees and charges, before a consumer commits to rent. The company also must stop withholding funds for ordinary wear and tear and is prohibited from misleading claims about property conditions.

The consumer redress funds created by the settlement total $48.5 million and will be used for relief as directed by the stipulated order entered in the federal case. Arizona is receiving $1.25 million.

In 2024, Invitation Homes, the largest owner of U.S. single-family rental homes, agreed to pay $48 million to consumers and change some of its practices.

Editor’s note: This story was updated with a statement from the FTC.

#5303. Opendoor says it’s behind schedule but plans to catch up by 2027

Opendoor reported a $66 million adjusted net loss and a $218 million net loss in Q3 2026, despite 12% revenue growth to $1.022 billion. The company said it is behind schedule on its profitability goal and is leaning on capital-light products, AI pricing and mortgage growth.  AI Summary

Opendoor is behind schedule. Since taking over the company a little over a year ago, CEO Kaz Nejatian has promised that the firm would achieve adjusted net income positive status on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026.

But the recent housing market downturn, triggered by the rapid rise in mortgage rates, has proven to be a bit of a roadblock. “We are currently behind but we intend to catch up,” the iBuyer’s third quarter 2026 earnings report explained.

During the quarter, Opendoor recorded an adjusted net loss of $66 million and an actual net loss of $218 million, up from a $90 million net loss a year ago. This comes even as the company reported a 12% annual increase in revenue to $1.022 billion.

“A year ago, I told you we would build a different Opendoor — faster, stronger, fully committed to our mission of tilting the world in favor of homeowners,” Nejatian said during his firm’s earnings call with investors and analysts on Thursday.

“We have spent the past year building a machine, and that machine is getting better every single day. We are not done yet. It is not perfect, but it is getting better every single day. The question is this: Is Opendoor in a better economic condition than it was a year ago? The answer is obviously yes.”

Nejatian’s confidence comes from his belief that Opendoor has become more resilient over the past year. This includes ways in which the company has worked to serve more sellers without adding more homes to the company’s balance sheet.

“This past week, around half of the first offers our direct-to-consumer sellers accepted were listing or Cash Now, More Later. That lets us serve more sellers with less of our capital exposed to changes in the market,” Nejatian said.

In the past 12 months, the company has done over $1 billion in Cash Now, More Later volume.

“We have built more ways to meet sellers’ needs and have made it easier for them to understand their options and make the choice they want for their own lives,” Nejatian said. “Sellers can now adjust the offer slides and make the choice that is good for their families.”

Nejatian noted that every other time Opendoor has tried to scale, it has done so by purchasing more properties, but that isn’t the case this time.

“We proved that we can grow without buying growth. That’s the single most important thing that has happened over the last year. We’re changing that with our capital-light products,” Nejatian said.

Still, Opendoor did purchase far more homes in Q3 2026 than it did in Q3 2025, with a 316% year-over-year increase to 4,865 homes. The company’s signed acquisition volume represented an estimated 0.56% of market share in the addressable U.S. market in Q3 2026 — more than four times higher than a year ago.

On the sales side, Opendoor sold 2,728 homes, an increase of 160 homes compared to a year ago. At the end of the quarter, the iBuyer had 7,596 homes in its inventory, up from 3,139 homes a year ago. While the increase in inventory could be seen as cause for concern, especially heading into the slower winter housing market, Opendoor noted that homes listed for sale for 120 days represented just 18% of inventory at the end of the quarter, down from 50% a year ago.

Despite the progress, Nejatian said the company still has work left to do on unit economics and resale velocity, something it needs to focus on as it strives for more resiliency.

“We’re not as good as we want to be, but we’re in a much better place,” he said. “When the market moves against you and you own homes, there’s two things you can do. You can sell fast, or you can hold and wait and pray for the market to recover. We choose to clear.

“The decline in late August and September knocked us off track on execution a little bit because we turned our attention to clearance rather than margin improvement. It costs something real in a quarter like this, but that’s the right way to run this company for the long run.”

To help with some of these challenges, Nejatian said Opendoor has turned to AI to help improve speed while still scaling. Some of these tools include an AI model that determines repair plans for every home to hit the market. The company said the system has been outperforming the old process of following a standard repair manual.

Opendoor said it also built a system to help price homes. While humans still have final judgment, the software does the work of pulling applicable, comparable homes.

Nejatian also said that Opendoor is focusing on its mortgage division. In Q3, Opendoor said originations from its in-house lender were up 400% year over year. This comes as the iBuyer’s lender is now licensed in 25 states, compared to none a year ago.

In addition, the company also launched a beta test of Buy with Opendoor in the San Francisco Bay Area this week. The product allows the company to earn mortgage revenue on properties not affiliated with Opendoor in anyway.

Looking to the future, Nejatian said Opendoor is hoping to build out title and escrow services — not only to add more efficiencies to Opendoor’s in-house transactions but to add additional revenue streams by serving consumers not in its ecosystem.

“We need to grow, use less capital per transaction, and sell homes faster. Those are things we can control, and that is what we are focused on. What matters to us is solving the core problems of our business, and those are what we need to focus on,” Nejatian said.

#5301. Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?

The October jobs report showed 165,000 payroll growth and a steady 4.1% unemployment rate, consistent with improved 2026 labor conditions. Yield direction was driven more by AI-related market swings and broader bond market levels, keeping mortgage rates near 7.17%.  AI Summary

With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well.

Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement.

From BLS:  Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing.The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed’s is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year.

Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it’s still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor.

This month’s report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad.

Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline?

One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet.

As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave’s stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break.

Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That’s good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today’s episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler.

A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows.
