#5299. Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but will Big Tech end up winning anyway?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?

The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.

Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer.

And the AI juggernaut indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.

All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.

Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time. We can walk and chew gum at the same time if we put our mind to it. Hard to imagine the Dems could do worse than Trump and the GOP have been doing for years now.

OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations That was quick; we’ll see if it makes a difference.

#5298. Mortgage rates fell and demand steadied as inventory dipped

Inventory declined week over week to 902,740 as mortgage rates eased for 3 straight weeks. With spreads at 2.27%, the path to sub-7% mortgage rates can happen with lower bond yields or better mortgage spreads.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates fell, demand stabilized and inventory had a noticeable decline last week. But are the changes in demand and inventory data about seasonality, or has the housing market changed with the recent mortgage rate decline? Let’s take a look at the weekend tracker and see what the data is telling us with rates falling the last three weeks.

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

What a crazy time in the bond market recently: the key level of 5.35% has not only held since early October, but the reversal has been truly nice to watch. The midterm elections, which changed the control of the House and Senate, have added another variable into the mortgage rate equation. I discussed what Congress can do to help lower mortgage rates on this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler, but for now the head-and-shoulders pattern of the 10-year yield is still somewhat intact, though a fight for it to break lower is happening.

I wouldn’t get too excited about mortgage rates until the 10-year yield can break under 4.70% and have follow-through bond buying, but mortgage rates have fallen and demand has stabilized over the last few weeks.

Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multiyear lows. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% —  spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility.That said, if mortgage spreads weren’t near multiyear lows right now, we’d have no chance of getting mortgage rates below 7.25%, and demand wouldn’t have stabilized recently. Now that spreads have moved up from this year’s lows, we can clearly see that mortgage rates would be sub-7% if spreads return to that level.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.27% from 2.23% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

The key for the last three weeks: lower rates, even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, this isn’t growth, just stabilization from a noticeable slowdown when mortgage rates got toward 7.60%. The last three years and 10 months show that housing demand grows when mortgage rates fall below 6.64% and head toward 6%; above 7%, we don’t have much growth data beyond seasonal demand. Last year at this time, mortgage rates were headed toward 6%, so the year-over-year comps will be hard for some time.

Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We had a small decline week to week; I can see the stabilization here as well and the year-over-year comps will also be very difficult here, as last year at this time rates were heading toward 6%. Earlier in the year, when rates were lower, pretty much every week this year showed growth.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks being down year over year. However, when mortgage rates got above 6.64% and then headed toward 7.60%, we did see some growth pick up. Also, rates were lower last year so demand was heading toward a nine-month high in December, which means it the comps will be easier to show growth in inventory.

Inventory growth is running at 7.18% even with easier comps.

New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 new listings per week a few times this year. The concern I had was that if higher rates cause sellers to stop listing their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 — that would hurt supply and demand. However, that hasn’t happened in any meaningful way. Most home sellers are buyers, and now that rates have fallen a smidge, it looks like we can end the year on a positive note for 2026 for new listings.

In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%; demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indexes show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown.

You want to keep an eye on how AI stocks trade this week, in particular CoreWeave’s stock price and how the 10-year yield reacts. For now, there’s an interesting correlation between the two, but I expect it to fade over time.

It’s inflation week again, with both CPI and PPI reports. Over the next 12 months, if the Iran conflict ends and the trade war doesn’t get worse, the question is whether bond traders will put more weight on those two factors than on the current inflation reports, which could improve in the future. This would be a huge positive for mortgage rates, but still, it will take a lot of work to end the trade war and the conflict. Existing home sales will come out and it won’t be pretty. We also have a lot of Fed speeches this week and it’s critical now to see what they say and how the bond market reacts to their talking points. Also, with the midterms over, I will be watching whether any of them start to talk about the end of the conflict and trade war being a positive for their future outlook.

#5297. Fibocom LTE Cat.1 bis Modules: Starlink DTC Field Test Report

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Nov. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fibocom's LE270-EU and LE271-GL LTE Cat.1 bis modules have successfully connected to the SpaceX Direct to Cell (DTC) satellite network during live-network testing in New Zealand. Using standard firmware and without adding satellite-specific hardware modifications, both modules successfully registered on the network, established IP data sessions, and transmitted data over the satellite link. Testing across outdoor, in-vehicle, and indoor environments also provided insights into real-world connectivity performance under different conditions.

Extending LTE Beyond Terrestrial Coverage

For asset trackers, environmental monitoring devices, and other IoT equipment deployed in remote agricultural areas, mountainous regions, or locations with limited cellular coverage, satellite connectivity offers an additional way to keep devices connected.

Traditionally, adding satellite capabilities can introduce additional hardware requirements, power consumption, and development costs. This raises an important question for IoT device manufacturers: Can existing LTE designs be extended to support satellite connectivity without adding dedicated satellite communication hardware?

LTE Cat.1 bis offers a practical balance of data performance, mobility, power consumption, and cost for a broad range of IoT applications. SpaceX Direct to Cell extends the reach of cellular technology by deploying LTE base station capabilities on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites and operating through partnerships with mobile network operators.

For compatible LTE devices that meet the relevant network access requirements, satellites can provide an additional connectivity option beyond terrestrial cell towers.

This creates opportunities for OEMs to explore satellite-enabled IoT applications while retaining their existing LTE hardware architecture, potentially reducing the complexity of introducing satellite connectivity into established device designs.

Real-World Performance Across Two Environments

Establishing a satellite connection is only part of the equation. For IoT applications, reliable data transfer and the ability to operate under varying coverage conditions are equally important.

Under open-sky conditions, both modules successfully established satellite data connections and demonstrated practical data throughput.

During outdoor and in-vehicle testing with good sky visibility, the LE270-EU achieved approximately 2.2 Mbps downlink throughput, while the LE271-GL reached approximately 2.0 Mbps. Both modules delivered around 0.3 Mbps uplink throughput, with network registration taking approximately 1â30 seconds and ping response rates ranging from 80% to 90%.

The modules were also able to register and exchange data under weak-signal conditions, demonstrating the feasibility of standard LTE connectivity over a live satellite network.

In indoor environments with obstructed sky visibility, connectivity performance varied more significantly.

When tested inside a hotel room, downlink throughput dropped to approximately 0.5 Mbps in some test scenarios, while ping response rates were around 65%â70%. Some data requests also experienced noticeably longer response times.

These findings highlight both the potential and the practical considerations of satellite-enabled IoT connectivity.

For applications such as asset tracking and agricultural monitoring, which typically transmit small amounts of data at regular intervals, the priority is not necessarily to match terrestrial LTE speeds. Instead, satellite connectivity can provide an additional path for transmitting location updates, device status, and sensor readings when terrestrial coverage is unavailable.

Extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks is valuable, but IoT devices must still meet fundamental requirements for size, power efficiency, and development cost, particularly in battery-powered applications designed to operate unattended for extended periods.

Fibocom's LE270 and LE271 series LTE Cat.1 bis modules feature a compact 17.7 Ã 15.8 Ã 2.4 mm form factor and Power Saving Mode (PSM) current as low as 2.5 Î¼A. With OpenCPU development capabilities and a range of peripheral interfaces, the modules offer flexibility for compact device designs, integrated applications, and power-sensitive IoT deployments.

Satellite connectivity also introduces different considerations for power management.

In the field tests, uploading the same file over the satellite connection required approximately 1.5â1.8 times the energy consumed over a terrestrial cellular connection. The increase was primarily associated with longer transmission times, higher transmit current, and data retransmissions. Meanwhile, the modules maintained their low PSM sleep current.

For battery-powered IoT devices, combining low-power hardware with an appropriate data reporting strategy is essential. Adjusting reporting intervals, buffering data during temporary connectivity interruptions, and retrying transmissions when the link becomes available can help devices operate more effectively under variable satellite network conditions.

The testing has also provided Fibocom with practical engineering insights into satellite network access, data transmission, and connectivity performance across different environments.

Building on these results, Fibocom is continuing to optimize DTC firmware compatibility for the LE270 and LE271 series, with a focus on improving network registration efficiency and connection resilience. These efforts will further support device manufacturers exploring satellite connectivity for asset tracking, remote monitoring, and other IoT applications.

Fibocom, founded in 1999, is China's first wireless communication module company listed on both the A-share and H-share markets. Fibocom leverages wireless communication and artificial intelligence as its core technologies to provide integrated hardware and software solutions that empower industry applications. These solutions accelerate the transformation from "Connect Everything" to "Intelligent Connectivity" across diverse industries.

Fibocom's one-stop solutions encompass cellular communication, AI, automotive, and GNSS modules, as well as AI toolchains, supporting industry-side and mainstream large model integration, and providing AI Agent, global connectivity, and cloud services, driving the digital intelligence upgrades in industries such as robotics, consumer electronics, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, smart retail, and smart energy.

#5295. What NAR’s new MLS policy options mean for data feeds and licensing

NAR adopted 4 MLS policy recommendations at NAR NXT 2026, including an optional policy that lets MLSs seek up to 50% copyright interest in certain listing content with opt outs. Additional updates address local rules for data feeds, permitted uses tied to brokerage or valuation services, and MLS Committee qualifications.  AI Summary

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) has approved four multiple listing service (MLS) policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee.

The recommendations from NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee were considered and adopted at NAR NXT 2026 conference on Sunday and are tied to the trade group’s 2026-2028 strategic plan to modernize MLS policies, the association said in an announcement Sunday.

The most consequential change for brokers and MLS operators is a revision to MLS Policy Statement 7.85 and the creation of a new optional policy on copyright protection of MLS data.

Under the revised policy, MLSs may, at their discretion, require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content to strengthen copyright enforcement, subject to quarterly copyright registration requirements. MLSs must give participants the right to opt out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS, and brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content.

Copyright ownership and enforcement have become more important as listing photos and data are syndicated across portals, IDX sites and marketing platforms, and as MLSs face more frequent questions and disputes about unauthorized scraping and reuse of listing content.

NAR also adopted an optional MLS policy on MLS data feed services. The policy allows MLSs to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, as long as those rules are reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants.

Even with new local rules, participants must retain access to MLS listing information and data feeds for their own listings.

For brokers and vendors, this could affect how quickly and under what conditions they can obtain broader data feeds for tools such as brokerage websites, back-office systems and analytics products, depending on how individual MLSs choose to implement the optional policy.

A new MLS policy statement reinforces that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and must be connected to real estate brokerage services, the preparation of appraisals or other valuations of real property.

NAR said this is intended to address concerns around unauthorized use of MLS content, including use cases that are not connected to providing brokerage or valuation services.

For MLSs, this language provides additional backing for enforcement actions against parties that use listing data for unrelated commercial purposes. For brokers and appraisers, it underscores the need to align technology partnerships and data workflows with the scope of their MLS agreements.

NAR also updated the qualification criteria for service on its MLS Committee. The changes are meant to better reflect today’s MLS environment and ensure the committee includes members with relevant industry expertise and perspectives.

While specific qualification details were not outlined in the announcement, changes to committee composition can influence how future policy recommendations are shaped and how regional and business-model interests are represented at the national level.

“These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective, and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” Nykia Wright, the CEO of NAR and a 2026 HousingWire Woman of Influence and Vanguard award winner, said in the announcement. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members, and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.”

Because several of the policies are optional, local MLSs will have to decide whether and how to adopt them. MLS executives and boards will likely review their copyright strategies, data feed agreements and committee engagement structures in light of the new framework.

Brokers, teams and technology vendors should review their MLS participation and data licensing agreements to understand how any local policy changes could affect website data feeds, marketing uses of listing content and third-party integrations.

#5292. NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment

NAR economist Lawrence Yun said pent-up housing demand could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves, and confidence rebounds. NAR data show existing-home sales near 4M, first-time buyers at 22%, and months’ supply at its highest since 2015.  AI Summary

The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans.

Yun contrasted today’s sales environment with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year, well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data.

“Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said.

On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR.

“Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.”

Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs.

“If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said.

Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40.

Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers.

“First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They’re also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.”

Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey.

“The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.”

Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent.

“Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said.

For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves.

For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints.

For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory. With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage.

Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to post-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs, making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond.

#5291. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5290. AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.

To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc,, who has some deep experience in this area.

As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.

She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.

When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family: Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.

The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:

The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AWS Supply Chain was such a useful learning experience. When Aubrey got close to the product, she saw a team working to catch up rather than lead. They had been building five modules that “largely were about getting to feature parity” with entrenched enterprise resource planning vendors that had a decades-long head start.

Connect had taken the opposite path, and it’s instructive. “They understood they weren’t going to achieve feature parity,” Aubrey said of the Connect team. Instead, they led with outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone, started narrow and built from there.

Aubrey applied that same lesson to the supply chain. She rebooted it as Connect Decisions by asking a different question: where is the pain most acute, and where is the current tooling weakest? The answer was planners. “They’re firefighting the whole time,” she said. “They’re overwhelmed by a whole bunch of signals. By the time they get to decide, the moment has passed.”

The same applies to enterprises. AI projects that stall often try to replicate an entire workflow. The ones that succeed identify a painful decision point and make it dramatically better.

Aubrey’s point about measurement deserves unpacking. “Companies are stuck on what’s the ROI of AI, and they’re looking at return on tokens and this sort of stuff,” she said. “The question is, can you move your business metrics by working in a different way?”

Her proof point is Wells Vehicle Electronics, which, according to AWS, cut inventory by 7% in three months while expanding the SKUs they actively monitor from 20 to 2,000. Nobody at Wells is talking about tokens. They’re talking about working capital. If a project can’t be tied to a metric the chief financial officer already tracks, it’s an experiment, not an investment.

Amazon started where most companies start: with software development, making AI tools available across the company. Aubrey admits there’s a bit of chaos at first. “Everyone’s just experimenting with a bunch of things,” Aubrey said.

She sees that as a feature, not a bug, because that’s where the real learning happens. “You go through this learning period of, you know what, our test coverage sucks,” she said. Fix test coverage, and you find “our pipelines suck,” so you fix pipeline health, eliminate manual intervention and deploy faster. The result in her group this year: a twofold improvement in the velocity of pushes to production.

The lesson is that the velocity didn’t come from the coding assistant. It came from fixing everything downstream that the assistant exposed. Enterprises that buy the tool and skip the plumbing will see activity rise while output stays flat.

I asked Aubrey whether Amazon has adjusted its goals to reflect what employees can now do with AI. Her answer was an honest “yes and no.” In her user experience team, roles have collapsed: designers are being pushed to ship code to an alpha environment, and Amazon has created a new “UX tech” role.

The “no” is that org design and goal-setting are still catching up. Her message to her team is blunt: “The only choice you can’t make is to own the task. You have to choose to own the outcome.” Every IT leader should borrow that line. Task-based job descriptions will age poorly.

AWS’s design philosophy for the Connect family is what she calls “humorphism,” the idea that AI should fit the way people already work, not the other way around. Her biggest concern is the lag between internal prototypes and production.

“Shipping good AI with a bad user experience will fail, in my opinion,” she said. Her team has invested heavily in closing that gap, moving beyond traditional command-based interfaces toward AI that picks up cues, remembers decisions, and carries work forward. The goal, she said, is to make AI so usable that people change how they work, not because they’re told to, but because it makes sense.

She was equally candid about maturity. TE Connectivity has scaled Connect Decisions to 2,000 planners, but Connect Talent reached general availability only in September and has early customers in deployment. Aubrey said the team is focused on getting the product right before aggressively scaling, reflecting the same “pick a wedge” discipline she applied across the Connect solutions.

What made this conversation valuable was Aubrey’s willingness to share how she thinks about building AI products that work in production, from studying what made Connect successful to applying those lessons across supply chain, hiring, health care, and customer engagement. That candor is a useful model for IT leaders, because most enterprise AI programs are stuck for the same reasons AWS’s applications once were: too much breadth, too little focus and success measured by the wrong yardstick.

The AI era won’t reward companies with the most pilots. It will reward those that pick a sharp problem, fix the plumbing it exposes, redesign work around outcomes and move the metrics they already have.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5285. Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa.

Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs.

Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. The company plans to release the model’s weights under an open-source license next week.

#5284. LG ELECTRONICS EARNS FIRST ASIL D PRODUCT CERTIFICATION FOR AUTOMOTIVE CENTRAL GATEWAY SYSTEM

TÃV Rheinland's First ASIL D Product Certification in the Central Gateway System Category Validates LG's Functional Safety Capabilities

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Electronics (LG) has earned its first ISO 26262 Automotive Safety Integrity Level D (ASIL D) product certification for its automotive central gateway system, developed as the central communication unit (CCU) 2.0 for the Genesis GV90. The certification, awarded by global testing and certification body TÃV Rheinland, is also the first ASIL D product certification the organization has issued in the automotive central gateway system category.*

Under ISO 26262, ASILs range from A to D based on the severity of potential harm, exposure to hazardous situations and controllability of the resulting risks. ASIL D, the highest level, requires the most stringent measures to prevent and mitigate safety-related failures. As part of the certification process, TÃV Rheinland comprehensively assessed LG's development processes, design documentation and verification results, confirming the system's compliance with applicable ASIL D requirements.

From Certified Processes to ASIL D-Certified Products

The certification is the latest step in LG's efforts to advance its functional safety capabilities. The company obtained ISO 26262 process certification for its automotive development framework in 2017, followed by ASIL B product certification for its advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) front camera module in 2021. Achieving ASIL D at the product level demonstrates LG's ability to apply the highest functional safety requirements across the design, implementation and verification of an automotive product.

For global automakers, this independent, product-level validation offers further assurance of LG's ability to deliver safety-critical automotive systems. It is also expected to enhance the company's competitiveness in future vehicle platform programs.

Functional Safety Embedded in System Operations

LG's central gateway system serves as the hub for vehicle communications, connecting electronic control units (ECUs) and managing data exchange across in-vehicle and external networks. When routing data over controller area network (CAN) and Ethernet interfaces, the system is designed to accurately transmit safety-related messages, detect routing malfunctions and relay relevant fault information to other ECUs.

The system also incorporates functional safety measures for over-the-air (OTA) software updates. These measures help prevent unintended updates and maintain safe control of vehicle start-up during updates and rollbacks. In addition, the system supports connected car services, features on demand and system diagnostics, along with cybersecurity functions such as intrusion monitoring and certificate-based authentication.

Strengthening Competitiveness for Future AIDV Platforms

As the automotive industry transitions toward AI-defined vehicles (AIDVs), central gateway systems are taking on a larger role. They manage communications across vehicle networks, enable OTA updates and support connected services, which makes functional safety increasingly critical.

The expertise LG gained through this project is applicable to other safety-critical automotive systems. That expertise spans functional safety development processes, design and verification methodologies, and certification. These capabilities lay the groundwork for LG to develop a broader range of automotive components, including next-generation communication control systems, gateways and domain controllers.

"Earning our first ASIL D product certification is a significant milestone for LG," said Lee Sang-yong, head of the VS R&D Laboratory at the LG Vehicle Solution Company. "It reflects our progress from establishing certified functional safety processes to implementing and verifying the highest-level safety requirements in an automotive product. We will build on this accomplishment to strengthen automakers' confidence in LG and advance next-generation solutions for the AIDV era."

* Based on TÃV Rheinland's certification records as of November 2026

#5283. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5282. LG ELECTRONICS EARNS FIRST ASIL D PRODUCT CERTIFICATION FOR AUTOMOTIVE CENTRAL GATEWAY SYSTEM

TÃV Rheinland's First ASIL D Product Certification in the Central Gateway System Category Validates LG's Functional Safety Capabilities

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Electronics (LG) has earned its first ISO 26262 Automotive Safety Integrity Level D (ASIL D) product certification for its automotive central gateway system, developed as the central communication unit (CCU) 2.0 for the Genesis GV90. The certification, awarded by global testing and certification body TÃV Rheinland, is also the first ASIL D product certification the organization has issued in the automotive central gateway system category.*

Under ISO 26262, ASILs range from A to D based on the severity of potential harm, exposure to hazardous situations and controllability of the resulting risks. ASIL D, the highest level, requires the most stringent measures to prevent and mitigate safety-related failures. As part of the certification process, TÃV Rheinland comprehensively assessed LG's development processes, design documentation and verification results, confirming the system's compliance with applicable ASIL D requirements.

From Certified Processes to ASIL D-Certified Products

The certification is the latest step in LG's efforts to advance its functional safety capabilities. The company obtained ISO 26262 process certification for its automotive development framework in 2017, followed by ASIL B product certification for its advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) front camera module in 2021. Achieving ASIL D at the product level demonstrates LG's ability to apply the highest functional safety requirements across the design, implementation and verification of an automotive product.

For global automakers, this independent, product-level validation offers further assurance of LG's ability to deliver safety-critical automotive systems. It is also expected to enhance the company's competitiveness in future vehicle platform programs.

Functional Safety Embedded in System Operations

LG's central gateway system serves as the hub for vehicle communications, connecting electronic control units (ECUs) and managing data exchange across in-vehicle and external networks. When routing data over controller area network (CAN) and Ethernet interfaces, the system is designed to accurately transmit safety-related messages, detect routing malfunctions and relay relevant fault information to other ECUs.

The system also incorporates functional safety measures for over-the-air (OTA) software updates. These measures help prevent unintended updates and maintain safe control of vehicle start-up during updates and rollbacks. In addition, the system supports connected car services, features on demand and system diagnostics, along with cybersecurity functions such as intrusion monitoring and certificate-based authentication.

Strengthening Competitiveness for Future AIDV Platforms

As the automotive industry transitions toward AI-defined vehicles (AIDVs), central gateway systems are taking on a larger role. They manage communications across vehicle networks, enable OTA updates and support connected services, which makes functional safety increasingly critical.

The expertise LG gained through this project is applicable to other safety-critical automotive systems. That expertise spans functional safety development processes, design and verification methodologies, and certification. These capabilities lay the groundwork for LG to develop a broader range of automotive components, including next-generation communication control systems, gateways and domain controllers.

"Earning our first ASIL D product certification is a significant milestone for LG," said Lee Sang-yong, head of the VS R&D Laboratory at the LG Vehicle Solution Company. "It reflects our progress from establishing certified functional safety processes to implementing and verifying the highest-level safety requirements in an automotive product. We will build on this accomplishment to strengthen automakers' confidence in LG and advance next-generation solutions for the AIDV era."

* Based on TÃV Rheinland's certification records as of November 2026

#5280. OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation

OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as sources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today.

The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.

It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.

Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal, one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.

The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well.

The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing.

In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending.

Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving.

#5278. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5277. Bitcoin ETF Outflows Hit $430M as Hong Kong Expands Its BTC Market

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin ETF outflows reached $430.2 million at the end of Thursday, as institutional investors continued withdrawing capital from US-listed spot products. Meanwhile, Hong Kong is expanding its crypto investment market, with four spot Bitcoin ETFs now available to investors.

Hong Kong’s private banking and wealth management assets reached HK$12.9 trillion ($1.65 trillion) in 2025, marking a 24% annual increase. Net fund inflows also climbed 79%, according to the latest Hong Kong Private Wealth Management Report 2026.

The contrasting developments put Hong Kong’s growing digital asset industry in focus. While American investors reduce exposure through listed products, Asian financial institutions are building new ways to access Bitcoin.

US spot Bitcoin ETF products recorded $430.2 million in net outflows on November 5. Fidelity’s FBTC led withdrawals with $199.9 million, followed by BlackRock’s IBIT at $105 million. Grayscale’s GBTC recorded another $49.9 million in withdrawals, while Franklin Templeton’s EZBC lost $32.9 million.

The latest session pushed November’s cumulative Bitcoin ETFs outflows to $869.8 million across four trading sessions. Net withdrawals across the latest seven finalized sessions reached approximately $1.36 billion.

That pressure follows a brief recovery on November 4, when the funds attracted $74.6 million. However, the latest withdrawals suggest institutional demand remains fragile.

The selling also comes as Bitcoin struggles to regain momentum. Investors are now watching if continued redemptions translate into further pressure on the underlying market.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Hong Kong already operates a dedicated Bitcoin ETF market, rather than simply preparing to introduce cryptocurrency investment products.

The city has four spot Bitcoin ETFs listed on its exchange:

Hong Kong also offers two futures-based products: the CSOP Bitcoin Futures ETF and Samsung Bitcoin Futures Active ETF.

The first three spot products launched on April 30, 2024, making Hong Kong an early Asian market for regulated Bitcoin investment products. MicroBit subsequently joined the market in August 2025.

However, Hong Kong’s Bitcoin ETF market is not immune to withdrawals. November month-to-date flow figures from a regional ETF tracker showed outflows of $5.71 million from ChinaAMC, $1.58 million from Bosera HashKey and $68,880 from Harvest.

These figures show that institutional appetite remains uneven across both markets. Hong Kong’s smaller ETF market has not yet demonstrated that it can absorb the selling pressure seen in the United States.

Nevertheless, the wider financial industry continues building its digital asset exposure.

According to the Hong Kong Private Wealth Management Report 2026, 43% of surveyed firms have added cryptocurrency ETFs or exchange-traded products to their offerings. Another 25% are developing digital asset trading platforms, custody services or product ranges, and a further 28% plan to invest in digital assets within the next two to three years.

Hong Kong’s wider asset management industry reached HK$42.2 trillion, according to the Securities and Futures Commission. This gives traditional financial institutions a substantial pool of capital from which to develop new investment products.

The longer-term opportunity extends beyond immediate Bitcoin ETF subscriptions. Hong Kong is developing an institutional ecosystem that includes regulated products, custody services, and established wealth management firms.

The latest US withdrawals show that institutional demand can reverse quickly. However, Hong Kong’s expanding infrastructure displays that the competition for digital asset capital across global financial centers is far from over.

#5276. ASMAX at EICMA 2026: Beyond the Next in Motorcycle Communication

MILAN, Nov. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ASMAX brought its vision of next-generation motorcycle communication to EICMA 2026 at Hall 6, Booth H08, unveiling a preview of its next-generation RoamX intercom, showcasing exclusive collaborations with ZXMOTO and WorldSSP racer Valentin Debise, and introducing new initiatives to make connected riding more accessible worldwide.

RoamX: A New Chapter in Riding Communication

At the center of the presentation was RoamX, the world's first screen-equipped motorcycle intercom headset, currently targeted for launch in 2027. Developed around a new-generation chip after more than two years of engineering, RoamX features an integrated display, Mesh communication for up to 32 riders, and an enhanced AI voice assistant. The functional prototypes showcase ASMAX's vision for more intuitive, intelligent and personalized riding experiences.

Bringing Mesh Within Reach of More Riders

Beyond flagship innovation, ASMAX highlighted its commitment to making advanced communication technology accessible to more motorcyclists. The ASMAX S2 combines Mesh communication with an approachable price point, offering an accessible entry into connected group riding. By lowering the barrier to Mesh technology, ASMAX aims to encourage more riders to experience the benefits of staying connected on the road.

EICMA also brought together two important ASMAX collaborators: Zhang Xue, Founder and CEO of ZXMOTO, and Valentin Debise, ASMAX Global Brand Ambassador and professional World Supersport rider.

The event showcased the ZXMOTO collaboration edition, featuring racing-inspired design, alongside the ASMAX Debise Racing Edition, a special collector's edition developed around the partnership with Valentin Debise. Together, these collaborations reflect the shared spirit of engineering, performance and passion that connects the motorcycle industry and its riders.

#5275. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”
