#5273. AI cyber resilience and the trust gap

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante and Krista Case

Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets.

In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake?

Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit.

Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes.

Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments.

We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions:

These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require.

Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI.

Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested.

These findings come from a small sample of in-depth interviews conducted with our partner Qualitate. The conversations allowed us to explore what customers have tested, the additional security work their own AI creates and what it takes to resume a business process safely. One healthcare practitioner phrased the disconnect between confidence and readiness as follows:

No, we have not completed any tabletop exercises as it pertains to an AI agent or other similar attacks. We’re highly confident because these are scenarios similar to non-AI incidents we have handled before.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Across the interviews, respondents who did express confidence often drew heavily on existing ransomware and incident response playbooks. Their experience with non-AI incidents understandably provides a degree of trust. But it also raises a concern in that organizations may assume that an agent taking an incorrect action can be handled in the same way as an insider or external attacker doing something similar. We don’t believe existing playbooks cover all scenarios.

Rather, we believe that assumption needs to be tested against the specific demands of an agent incident. The interviews revealed a mixed picture of true validation:

Complete business recovery requires an organization to reconstruct a sequence of authorized actions, identify incorrect outcomes, repair downstream effects and safely resume the affected business process. Demonstrating that the full sequence works is a nontrivial exercise.

The speed, scale and interconnected nature of agent activity makes that even more challenging. Actions can affect multiple systems and processes, creating consequences that existing playbooks need to account for. We see a risk of false confidence when organizations assume that their experience with traditional non-AI incidents will translate automatically. Testing needs to establish how well their capabilities hold up under the conditions an agent can create, which may be novel.

Bottom line: Evidence of validated, end-to-end business recovery from an agent incident remains limited in our study. We believe organizations should exercise their existing playbooks against realistic agent scenarios, with safe business resumption as the measure of success.

Our interviews raised questions about tooling, maturity and the processes needed to prove that existing capabilities work for agentic AI. Two findings as shown below highlight the limited reach of detection and reconstruction capabilities in the organizations studied:

One healthcare practitioner’s assessment of the controls already implemented underscores the trust gap:

No, for the ones that have been implemented, we have not tested or validated that they work.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Enterprises already have identity systems, application logs, data protection tools and the like, along with established incident response processes. They are trying to extend these capabilities to AI. The central challenge is validating that the tools can reconstruct activity across an entire agent workflow.

Agents interact with multiple applications, invoke tools and autonomously trigger downstream actions. Each system may capture its own events without providing a coherent record of the complete workflow. Incident response requires correlating those records to establish which agent acted and under what authority, then tracing the tools it invoked and the changes that resulted.

This reminds us of the early days of disaster recovery, when organizations would test failover but hesitate to test failback because they were nervous about what might happen. We see a similar reluctance to ask questions that could expose gaps in readiness or cause downstream problems. The concern is whether the connected tools and processes will hold up under realistic agent incident conditions.

Bottom line: Organizations need to exercise the full agent workflow under realistic conditions, including a plausible worst-case event, and validate that their tools and processes can reconstruct the activity and support the response.

Our assessment of the field interviews highlights both the technical and business dimensions involved in a recovery. An AI agent can use legitimate access to change a record incorrectly or send a message that should never have been sent. A backup may work and the restored systems may appear healthy while the business remains unable to resume safely.

StorageTek veteran Fred Moore, an early mentor to Dave Vellante, coined the phrase: “Backup is one thing, recovery is everything.” The scope of recovery continues to expand as organizations consider the consequences of agents acting across business systems.

A director of information security at a media and entertainment firm described the problem this way:

We could restore our systems, we could restore within our recovery objectives, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that it’s safe. The bottleneck here would be trust.

— Director of information security, media and entertainment

Recovery point objectives or RPO and recovery time objectives or RTO are the so-called business metrics. But business users need more meaningful key performance indicators that resonate — specifically, what a trusted, viable service looks like and how that condition can be verified. That includes establishing who needs to participate in recovery and who signs off that operations can safely resume.

This direction needs to come from the top down; and be verified bottom up. Business leaders must define the requirements, with IT and security acting as partners to provide the underlying technology and help achieve the required outcome. The responsibility extends beyond the traditional data protection team’s work of recovering data and systems.

Incorrect transactions, human error and failures that ripple across systems have existed for a long time. Agentic AI adds two complications:

That requires a comprehensive view of what went wrong and what needs to happen to recover. The organization must be able to trace the agent’s activity and evaluate the resulting business state against clear criteria for safe operation.

Bottom line: Recovery requires explicit criteria for verifying that a business service can be trusted and clear responsibility for approving its return to operation. The business must set that direction, with IT and security providing the capabilities to carry it out.

Humans in the loop help organizations restrict what agents can do. Resilience also has to account for what happens when a human misses an incorrect action or cannot keep pace with agents operating at machine speed. Two statements from the same CIO illustrates the issue:

So the given scenario will be detected by human beings before the AI agents can take the actions.

If it really happens, currently we do not have the capability to roll back the agent’s action.

— Chief information officer, real estate and construction

The first statement shows confidence that human oversight will catch the problem. The second acknowledges a missing “undo command” if the human oversight fails. This captures why approvals and recovery testing need to advance together. Reliance on human intervention can bring a false sense of security and defer attention to the recovery details needed when a mistake gets through.

Our field study also revealed how customers are weighing the tradeoffs around autonomy, with organizations generally still containing what their agents can do. Those decisions become particularly important when agents receive authority to take remedial actions during an incident or recovery.

The level of autonomy granted should reflect the risk of the action. Before allowing an agent to approve or execute a remedial action, organizations need to understand the consequences of an incorrect decision. That calls for a tiered approach built around two considerations:

We expect human approval to become an increasingly significant bottleneck over the next six to 12 months. Organizations need to establish these boundaries as they begin trusting agents to take more remedial actions.

Bottom line: Human oversight and recovery testing need to develop together. As organizations delegate more authority to agents, they must account for mistakes, the limits of human review and the risk associated with each action.

A retail practitioner described a viable approach to rehearsing an agent incident and we see this as a best practice. Specifically, this firm replays the agent’s actions in a replica environment, investigating the root cause and using granular snapshots to understand the transactional effects. The respondent explicitly confirmed that the approach had been tested in the sandbox with the following statement:

Yes, if the agent went across multiple systems, my approach is to replay this within my sandbox environment, which is a full replica of all of the systems.

— Director of information technology, retail

The value of this approach is in reproducing the sequence of events and investigating their effects across systems. Our assessment of what such an exercise should confirm is anchored on three outcomes:

We see these as minimum viable expectations for the evidence an exercise should produce.

We use the term digital twin here as a broad analogy for this approach. A fuller digital twin would involve a richer representation of business processes, dependencies and state. We believe the industry still has work to do in that direction, and that work will become more important as enterprises use AI to run critical functions. In addition, it will further expand the notion of recovery as the state of the business will become increasingly more complicated as agents perform more of the work.

The respondent also acknowledged a limitation saying: larger transaction volumes could require more time for reconciliation. Replaying actions and identifying affected transactions provides useful information, while the time needed to resolve their consequences remains an open item. Richer simulations of business environments could help organizations test agent behavior and prepare for what a failure might look like in production.

In other words, testing the recovery sequence in a variety of scenarios inside a digital twin of the business prior to pushing the process into production. Further, this “red teaming” exercise must be ongoing – expanding the concept of continuous data protection into the state of a firm’s operations in more granular snapshots.

Bottom line: This example offers a practical approach to reproducing agent actions, investigating their consequences and rehearsing recovery. Its value also points toward the need for richer representations of the business processes those agents affect.

If a chief information security officer takes one action from this study, we recommend exercising an agent incident affecting one consequential workflow already in production. Choose a workflow in which an agent has permission to act across multiple systems, and design the exercise to include incorrect actions taken with valid credentials and permissions.

The exercise should also include a scenario requiring human approval. This helps establish the boundaries around where autonomy is appropriate and where human oversight remains necessary.

Validation by the business owner is essential. Security teams can establish that an incident has been contained and provide evidence of what happened. The business owner must determine whether the resulting business state is acceptable. That decision needs to account for the consequences of the agent’s actions and any remediation work still required.

The exercise should document what was proved, what remains untested and which teams are responsible for closing the remaining gaps. That evidence should also inform decisions about how much authority an agent receives. The organization needs to understand its ability to reverse or correct actions and recover their consequences as it considers granting greater autonomy.

The discussions at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit reinforced the themes emerging from the field study. Conversations with vendors, practitioners and researchers underscored the need to build resilience and recovery into agent deployments from the outset. Evidence that these capabilities work becomes essential as agentic workloads move into production.

The challenge includes preserving and recovering a trusted business state when an agent produces an incorrect outcome despite having legitimate credentials. Organizations need to understand how those outcomes affect their operations and what it will take to address them.

Existing investments in data protection infrastructure, security and recovery remain critical. The work ahead is to identify the gaps that emerge under the new requirements and pressures created by enterprise AI. That requires collaboration across internal teams and with vendors to understand where capabilities need to improve.

Bottom line: We believe trust in enterprise AI requires tested evidence that organizations can understand what agents have done, stop them, reconstruct their actions and recover to a healthy business state. Our research indicates that organizations still have work to do to demonstrate that their existing security and recovery capabilities can meet that requirement.

#5271. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5270. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5268. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

A Global Distributed Network Underpinning Secure, Accelerated Delivery

Built on more than 3,200 edge nodes across over 70 countries and a backbone network of more than 400 Tbps, EdgeOne carries both inbound China traffic and international traffic, delivering a low-latency, highly resilient digital experience that serves as a network cornerstone for enterprises expanding overseas or entering the Chinese market.

#5266. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5265. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to having extramarital affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia Corp. said on Sunday it’s launching an “independent investigation” into reports that its founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence plot, shortly after he admitted he “had been intimate” with a Singapore-based executive whom U.S. officials accuse of spying for China.

In response to the allegations, the Republican-led foreign affairs and intelligence committee of the U.S. Congress has asked Huang (pictured, right) to testify this week at a closed-door briefing on the chipmaker’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.” The request came after the New York Times reported last month that the CEO had been targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.

The accused spy is a woman called Alice Huang or Huang Le (left), of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. Alice Huang is the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed. It had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s high-end graphics processing units to China, prompting U.S. officials to begin monitoring her. Those officials have apparently determined that Alice Huang is an asset of the Chinese intelligence services, tasked with passing commercial secrets back to Beijing.

In a statement earlier today, Nvidia’s board of directors said that though it has no reason to believe that either U.S. national security or the company’s secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the statement said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The company added that Huang supports the investigation into what happened and has vowed to cooperate fully.

A report by Axios earlier today cited a draft email written by Huang to company employees, in which he admitted to having an illicit romantic relationship with Alice Huang and took full responsibility for his actions. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

U.S. intelligence chiefs will be concerned because Nvidia’s powerful chips sit at the center of the artificial intelligence boom and give America a critical advantage over its geopolitical rivals. The company’s dominance of AI computing means that Huang is one of the most influential people in the industry, and he has forged close ties with the Trump administration.

The alleged spy reportedly tried to take advantage of Huang’s close links to America’s policymakers. Not only was she tasked with learning more about the company’s secrets, but also persuading Huang to lobby for the company to be allowed to ship its most advanced processors to China.

It’s not clear how much influence she was able to exert on Huang, but last year he successfully petitioned the Trump administration to allow more GPUs to be exported to China. He later struck a deal to sell limited numbers of the company’s second-most powerful chips to China.

So far, nothing has been said of Huang potentially losing his job or being removed from the company, but Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives told Gizmodo that such an outcome is possible. “This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” the analyst said.

The investigation follows a rough week for technology firms on Wall Street, which have weathered a selloff that began earlier this month and gained traction after a series of disappointing earnings results in recent days. So far this month, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index has lost almost $1 trillion in value.

Nvidia’s stock has fallen 21% over the last month and is now basically flat in the year to date. Its market capitalization sits at just over $4.5 trillion, down from its peak of just over $5.7 trillion in October.

#5264. SOHU.COM REPORTS THIRD QUARTER 2026 UNAUDITED FINANCIAL RESULTS

BEIJING, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sohu.com Limited (NASDAQ: SOHU) ("Sohu" or the "Company"), a leading Chinese online media platform and game business group, today reported unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

Dr. Charles Zhang, Chairman and CEO of Sohu.com Limited, commented, "In the third quarter of 2026, our marketing services revenues hit the high end of our guidance, while both our online game revenues and our bottom-line performance were in line with our expectations. For the Sohu social media platform, we continued to strengthen its social features through numerous iconic events, fostering genuine connections among users and boosting active user interactions across multiple verticals. We also kept leveraging our integrated product matrix with innovative and customized marketing solutions to unlock monetization potential. For our online games, we continued to introduce fresh content to sustain player interest while offering tailored gameplay experiences to meet evolving player needs."

Total revenues were US$133 million, down 26% year-over-year and 2% quarter-over-quarter.

Marketing services revenues were US$15 million, up 10% year-over-year and down 2% quarter-over-quarter.

Online game revenues were US$114 million, down 30% year-over-year and 2% quarter-over-quarter.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP total cost of revenues were US$32 million, down 9% year-over-year and up 9% quarter-over-quarter.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP cost of marketing services revenues were US$15 million, up 23% year-over-year and 11% quarter-over-quarter.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP cost of online game revenues were US$14 million, down 33% year-over-year and up 2% quarter-over-quarter.

[1] Changyou's wholly-owned subsidiary Shanghai Jingmao Culture Communication Co., Ltd. ("Shanghai Jingmao"), which operated Changyou's cinema advertising business, ceased operations and commenced bankruptcy proceedings during the third quarter of 2019. During the third quarter of 2023, Shanghai Jingmao's bankruptcy proceedings were concluded by a Chinese mainland bankruptcy court, and the Company accordingly recognized a disposal gain within discontinued operations in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. During the second quarter of 2026, as a result of the Company's receipt of a further distribution of Shanghai Jingmao's insolvent assets, the Company recognized an additional disposal gain of US$1 million within discontinued operations in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. Unless indicated otherwise, results presented in this press release are related to continuing operations only and exclude the disposal gain mentioned above.

[2] Non-GAAP results exclude share-based compensation expense. Explanation of the Company's non-GAAP financial measures and related reconciliations to GAAP financial measures are included in the accompanying "Non-GAAP Disclosure" and "Reconciliations of Non-GAAP Results of Operation Measures to the Nearest Comparable GAAP Measures."

Both GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses were US$120 million, down 9% year-over-year and 4% quarter-over-quarter.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP operating losses were US$18 million, compared with operating profit of US$14 million in the third quarter of 2025 and an operating loss of US$18 million in the second quarter of 2026.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP income tax expenses were US$4 million, compared with income tax expense of US$17 million in the third quarter of 2025 and income tax benefit of US$7 million in the second quarter of 2026. For the second quarter of 2026, income tax benefit included reversal of a tax expense of approximately US$13 million due to a reversal of uncertain tax positions.

GAAP net loss attributable to Sohu.com Limited was US$15 million, or a net loss of US$0.60 per fully-diluted American depositary share ("ADS," each ADS representing one Sohu ordinary share), compared with net income of US$9 million in the third quarter of 2025 and net income of US$0.2 million in the second quarter of 2026.

Non-GAAP net loss attributable to Sohu.com Limited was US$15 million, or a net loss of US$0.59 per fully-diluted ADS, compared with net income of US$9 million in the third quarter of 2025 and net income of US$0.5 million in the second quarter of 2026.

As of September 30, 2026, cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments and long-term time deposits totaled approximately US$1.2 billion.

Supplementary Information for Changyou Results[3]

Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

Total revenues were US$115 million, a decrease of 30% year-over-year and 2% quarter-over-quarter. Online game revenues were US$114 million, a decrease of 30% year-over-year and 2% quarter-over-quarter. For online game revenues, the year-over-year decrease was mainly due to a natural decline from a high comparison base driven by content updates released for TLBB PC and the launch of TLBB: Return in the third quarter of 2025.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP total cost of revenues were US$14 million, a decrease of 33% year-over-year and an increase of 2% quarter-over-quarter.

Both GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses were US$42 million, a decrease of 23% year-over-year and 12% quarter-over-quarter. The year-over-year decrease was mainly due to a decrease in salary and benefits expenses, as well as a decrease in marketing and promotional spending for our online games. The quarter-over-quarter decrease was mainly due to a decrease in licensing fees related to product development.

GAAP operating profit was US$58 million, compared with US$87 million for the third quarter of 2025 and US$55 million for the second quarter of 2026.

Non-GAAP operating profit was US$59 million, compared with US$88 million for the third quarter of 2025 and US$56 million for the second quarter of 2026.

[3] "Changyou Results" consist of the results of Changyou's online game business and its 17173.com Website.

Under the previously-announced share repurchase program of up to US$150 million of the outstanding ADSs, Sohu had repurchased 10.1 million ADSs for an aggregate cost of approximately US$134 million as of November 5, 2026.

To supplement the unaudited consolidated financial statements presented in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America ("GAAP"), Sohu's management uses non-GAAP measures of operating profit/(loss), net income/(loss), net income/(loss) attributable to Sohu.com Limited and diluted net income/(loss) attributable to Sohu.com Limited per ADS, which are adjusted from results based on GAAP to exclude the impact of share-based compensation expense. These measures should be considered in addition to results prepared in accordance with GAAP, but should not be considered a substitute for, or superior to, GAAP results.

Sohu's management believes excluding share-based compensation expense from the Company's non-GAAP financial measures is useful for itself and investors. Further, the impact of share-based compensation expense could not be anticipated by management and business line leaders, and these expenses were not built into the annual budgets and quarterly forecasts that have been the basis for information Sohu provides to analysts and investors as guidance for future operating performance. As share-based compensation expense does not involve subsequent cash outflow and is not reflected in the cash flows at the equity transaction level, Sohu does not factor in its impact when evaluating and approving expenditures or when determining the allocation of its resources to its business segments. As a result, in general, the monthly financial results for internal reporting and any performance measures for commissions and bonuses are based on non-GAAP financial measures that exclude share-based compensation expense.

The non-GAAP financial measures are provided to enhance investors' overall understanding of Sohu's current financial performance and prospects for the future. A limitation of using non-GAAP operating profit/(loss), net income/(loss), net income/(loss) attributable to Sohu.com Limited, and diluted net income/(loss) attributable to Sohu.com Limited per ADS excluding share-based compensation expense is that this expense has been and can be expected to continue to recur in Sohu's business. In order to mitigate these limitations Sohu has provided specific information regarding the GAAP amounts excluded from each non-GAAP measure. The accompanying tables include details on the reconciliation between the GAAP financial measures that are most directly comparable to the non-GAAP financial measures that have been presented.

Financial information in this press release other than the information indicated as being non-GAAP is derived from Sohu's unaudited financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP.

We caution you that a number of important factors could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in any forward-looking statement. #5263. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

#5262. GreenCore Solutions Rebrands as WeFetch.ai for the AI Shopping Market: gtinfetch.ai lead product

AI sector in 2026: 3 billion AI users, half of consumers AI shopping, 8 in 10 buyers in leading sectors on AI agents, $2.7 trillion in AI spending

VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GreenCore Solutions Corp. (GSC) today announced it is rebranding as WeFetch.ai, a maker of artificial intelligence (AI) software for AI shopping, with 84 million barcodes across 70 countries live for AI agent shopping by consumers, retailers and brands.

The turn came in November 2025, when Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.5. GSC's management team recognized a confluence of events:

AI commerce has arrived, and it relies on gtinfetch.ai or similar AI software products to execute reliable transactions over x402, the new financial system's payment protocol.

One record for every product an AI agent might buy, keyed on the barcode, the Global Trade Item Number (GTIN). It answers only when the sources agree, and says "unknown" rather than guess. Around that record, a door for each party in AI shopping:

It offers a promotional and paid per answer model over x402.

WeFetch.ai, the barcode fetch system for AI agents. It answers for 84 million products in 70 countries, with 3.5 million points of sale on its own record, and includes:

It is AI native, and works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, Perplexity and Muse. Every answer is signed.

"I am pleased to announce to shareholders that we moved early into the AI agent market," said Matthew Keddy, Chief Executive Officer. "In the 11 months of 2026, AI reached 3 billion users, and 8 in 10 buyers in leading sectors went to AI agents. Those companies broke from the trendline. The 2 in 10 manufacturers still starting out are 4 times behind, 2 to 5 years back, and facing a specialist gap. In this market, behind stays behind: customers have moved to trading through AI agents, and the laggards lose value and velocity."

"We read the same signals everyone else had, and we acted. We treated the arrival of AI agents as a fiduciary matter for our shareholders; doing nothing would have been the mistake. We called it with the 8 in 10. The 2 in 10 stood still and watched. Today, we lead. With WeFetch, millions of AI agents can work with our barcode (GTIN) algorithm in real time, every transaction checked twice and recorded in our Record of Cleared Orders (RCO). Structural change this deep rarely happens in under 12 months. We saw it coming, we built for it, and we got it right."

The market: Gartner forecasts $2.7 trillion in AI spending in 2026. McKinsey projects that AI agents will orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion in global commerce by 2030, up to $1 trillion of it in US retail. Every one of those AI agent purchases needs the right barcode.

WeFetch.ai is AI software for AI shopping, with products for shopping, retail and brands. Powered by gtinfetch.ai, WeFetch.ai is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

#5261. Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm

— After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon.

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.

His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”

— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon. She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup Lila Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.

— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.

“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said. “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”

Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy. She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.

— Seattle-based RevealDx,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy, a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.

— Julie Averill, former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board, which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.

— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson, a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.

— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente, where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

#5260. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5258. Warren Buffett says ‘accumulating great amounts of money’ doesn’t achieve greatness—He still lives in a $31,500 Nebraska home and clipped coupons

Many entrepreneurs strive to one day add “millionaire,” or even “billionaire,” to their list of achievements: It’s a sign that they’ve finally made it in business. But billionaire investing mogul Warren Buffett hit back at the notion that eye-watering net worths equate to excellence.

“Greatness does not come about through accumulating great amounts of money, great amounts of publicity or great power in government,” Buffett wrote in his final Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter last November.

The 96-year-old “Oracle of Ohama,” known as one of the most successful investors of all time, is the 10th richest person in the world, boasting a fortune of $163 billion. But that doesn’t mean he’s splurging on mansions and driving luxury cars off the lot. He’s been thrifty throughout his seven-decade professional career, despite adding billions to his name.

Known for eating at McDonald’s, driving a beat-up old car, and living in his modest Nebraska home, it’s clear his bank account hasn’t changed his ways. Instead of feeling powerful by lavishing in the spoils of his riches, Buffett finds true value and greatness in non-material pursuits.

“When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world,” Buffett continued. “Kindness is costless but also priceless. Whether you are religious or not, it’s hard to beat The Golden Rule as a guide to behavior…Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman.”

Buffett’s golden rule is that everyone should be treated with kindness and respect, no matter if they’ve built a unicorn company, or are a junior-level worker. And he has treated the world’s most powerful business leaders the same way, unwilling to shell out on fancy meals to impress them.

The Berkshire Hathaway icon is known for stopping by McDonald’s for a cheap eat, choosing to order two sausage patties, an egg and cheese, or a bacon egg and cheese—all less than $4. He loves the fast-food chain so much he even took Bill Gates there for lunch years ago, instead of wining and dining him at a swanky restaurant. One time, the entrepreneurial pair were at a McDonald’s in Hong Kong, and Gates recalled laughing when Buffett offered to foot the measly bill, pulling coupons out of his pocket. But for the hedge-fund mogul, every penny counts.

The same money philosophy applies to Buffett’s major life purchases. The former CEO still lives in the same five bedroom, two-and-a-half bathroom Omaha home he bought for $31,500 back in 1958. The house would be worth around $1.4 million today—far more affordable than the luxurious pads Buffett can afford—yet he said he “wouldn’t trade it for anything.” Buffett’s true fondness for the home lies in the memories of raising his three kids on the property, not its market value.

Uber-rich people boasting net worths like Buffett may also be tempted to ball out on indulgences like expensive cars. But the investing magnate isn’t interested in getting behind the wheel of a Lamborghini or Aston Martin; he once drove a 20-year-old car because he felt it was safer than driving a speedy luxury alternative. And at one point, his license plate even read as “THRIFTY.”

Whether it be mansions or sports cars, Buffett steers clear of making major purchases that reflect his bank account. In fact, he feels giving in could be counterproductive to his happiness.

“I do not think that standard of living equates with cost of living beyond a certain point,” Buffett said at a Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in 2014. “My life would not be happier…it’d be worse if I had six or eight houses or a whole bunch of different things I could have. It just doesn’t correlate.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on November 12, 2025.
